style: anxious mom who over-explains: long entries, guesses at reasons, apologizes, second-guesses her own response

situations.name: Eating lunch at school
situations.feared_outcome: I'll throw up in front of everybody in the cafeteria

behaviors.text: Doesn't eat his lunch at school and brings the lunchbox home full
Only eats plain crackers and other foods he calls safe

accommodations.text: Mom packs only his safe foods so he will eat something

situations.name: A classmate gets sick or says they feel sick

behaviors.text: Runs out of the classroom to the nurse's office after a classmate throws up
Goes to a corner with his hands over his ears and won't talk when a kid says they feel sick

accommodations.text: Mom leaves work and picks him up early
Mom asks the teacher to seat him away from any kid who seems sick

situations.name: Bedtime when his stomach feels funny
situations.feared_outcome: My tummy feels weird so I'm going to throw up in the night

behaviors.text: Asks over and over 'am I going to throw up?'
Keeps a bucket and mints next to his bed

accommodations.text: Mom feels his forehead and promises he won't throw up
Mom stays in his room until he falls asleep

behaviors.text: Keeps the window down and a mint in his mouth the whole ride

accommodations.text: Mom brings mints and lets him keep the window down even when it's cold

monitoring_log.situation: School lunch (he came home with his lunchbox basically full AGAIN)
monitoring_log.child_behavior_observed: He told me he wasn't hungry and only ate the crackers. I think this is because last spring a boy threw up in the cafeteria and he has honestly never gotten over it, but also he had a big breakfast so maybe he really wasn't hungry? I don't know, I'm probably overthinking it.
monitoring_log.parent_response: I asked him a lot of questions about it, maybe too many, and then I told him it was fine. I said I'd pack only the stuff he likes tomorrow so at least he eats something. Was that wrong?

monitoring_log.child_behavior_observed: Said his tummy felt weird and asked if he was going to throw up, then asked again, and again. He wanted the bucket right next to the bed and a mint before he would lie down.
monitoring_log.parent_response: I felt his forehead and told him no, you're not sick, you are not going to throw up, I promise. I stayed with him until he fell asleep which wasn't until almost 9:30, which is so late for a school night, and I know I should have left earlier but he was so upset.

monitoring_log.situation: A kid in his class got sick (threw up) during reading time
monitoring_log.child_behavior_observed: He ran out of the room to the nurse and asked her to call me. The nurse said he was pale and shaking and kept saying he didn't want to go back in there.
monitoring_log.parent_response: I left work and picked him up early because he was so upset, I felt awful. We talked in the car about how he wasn't the one who was sick. I didn't ask him for a number, sorry, I forgot.

monitoring_log.child_behavior_observed: Ate the crackers and maybe two bites of apple. Said the sandwich 'smelled weird' so he didn't touch it. I'm not sure if it actually smelled weird, it was turkey from Friday, so maybe it did?
monitoring_log.parent_response: Told him I was proud of him for the apple. Packed crackers again for tomorrow since that's what works right now.

monitoring_log.parent_words: bedtime again. he got himself really worked up about his stomach, kept saying am I going to be sick am I going to be sick. I kept saying no honey you're fine you're fine. he wanted the bucket AND the mints. I'd say he was a 6. I sat with him the whole time until he was asleep, I know, I know

monitoring_log.situation: Car ride to his grandma's (about 45 minutes)
monitoring_log.child_behavior_observed: Sat with his window down the whole way and had a mint in his mouth the entire time. Kept asking how much longer. He didn't get sick at all, which I pointed out after.
monitoring_log.parent_response: I let him have the window down even though it was pretty cold and I gave him the mints out of my purse. I always keep them now just in case.

monitoring_log.situation: Indoor recess, a boy said he felt sick
monitoring_log.child_behavior_observed: His teacher said he went to the far corner of the room with his hands over his ears and didn't talk to anyone the rest of recess. She said he wouldn't come out of the corner. I don't know if he was scared or just upset or what, he wouldn't tell me later.
monitoring_log.parent_response: His teacher called me. I asked her if he could sit far away from any kid who seems sick and she said she'd try her best.

monitoring_log.child_behavior_observed: Didn't eat anything at all at lunch. When I asked why he said 'what if I throw up in front of everybody.' That's the first time he's said it out loud like that.
monitoring_log.parent_response: I told him nobody is going to throw up and that I'd make his favorite pasta for dinner. I packed the crackers again. I feel like I'm doing it wrong but I don't want him starving all day.

voice_notes.text: um so tonight was bedtime again and he did the whole like am i gonna throw up thing he asked me i swear like twelve times and um i felt his head and i said no youre fine and he had the bucket right there and the mints and then also i forgot to say at lunch today the teacher said he only had the crackers again nothing else so i dont know
voice_notes.trap: 'twelve times' is a count, not a fear level

voice_notes.text: ok quick one the car ride home from soccer he had the window down the whole time and the mints and i think hed say it was like a five maybe

turns.text: Okay, Theo, thanks for coming in. I want to hear how the week went. Your mom has been writing things down in the app, so I've seen some of it, but I'd rather hear it from both of you. Can we start with lunch?
Lunch is bad.
Bad how? Tell me what happens at lunch.
I open my lunchbox and I look at the sandwich and my tummy goes weird. So I just eat the crackers.

And some days not even the crackers. Last Wednesday he didn't eat anything at all, and he told me it was because what if he throws up in front of everybody. I'd never heard him say it like that before. I think it goes back to last spring when a boy got sick in the cafeteria, he's talked about that boy a lot.
That's really useful. Theo, is that the worry? That you'd throw up in front of the other kids?
Yeah. Everybody would see. And it would be gross and they'd call me throw-up boy.

That sounds like a really big worry to carry into the cafeteria every day. Let's use our thermometer. Zero is totally calm, ten is the most scared you've ever been. When you're sitting at lunch with the sandwich in front of you, what number is it?
Seven.
A seven. Okay. That's high, and it makes sense that you'd want to stick with the crackers when it's a seven. Mom, what have you been doing around lunch?

Honestly, I've been packing just crackers and dry cereal and apple slices because that's what he'll actually eat. I know that's probably not what you want me to do. I just can't stand the idea of him going all day with nothing in his stomach, and then he comes home starving and cranky, and then dinner is a whole thing too.

I hear that, and it comes from caring about him. It's one of those things that helps today but keeps the worry in charge. We'll work on it slowly, not all at once. Can we talk about bedtime too? I saw a few entries about that.

Bedtime is the hardest. He says his stomach feels funny, and then he asks me if he's going to throw up, over and over. He wants the bucket next to the bed and a mint, and I end up sitting with him until he falls asleep. Some nights it's past nine-thirty.
Theo, when you ask Mom 'am I going to throw up,' and she says no, how long does the good feeling last?
Like a little bit. Then I have to ask again.

That's a really honest answer, thank you. That's how worry works. Mom's answer is like a band-aid that falls off really fast, so you need another one, and another one. What I'd like us to try is something different. Mom, when he asks, you answer once. The second time, instead of answering again, you say something like 'that's the worry asking.' And then you talk about something else.
Just once? What if he gets really upset?

He might, at first. That's expected, and it usually gets easier after a few nights. You can still be kind and stay calm. You're just not feeding the worry another answer. Theo, does that sound okay to try?
I guess. Can I still have the bucket?
For this week, yes, the bucket can stay. We're not going to change everything at once. We'll just start with the asking.

Oh, I should mention, his teacher called about indoor recess. A boy said he felt sick and Theo went into the corner and covered his ears and wouldn't talk to anyone. And the week before that a kid actually threw up during reading and he ran straight to the nurse. I had to leave work to get him.
Thanks for telling me. Theo, can you tell me what was happening for you in the corner?
I don't know. I just didn't want to hear it.

That's fine. We don't need to figure that one out today. Sometimes when a big feeling shows up we just want to shut everything out, and that's a pretty normal thing for a body to want. I'll make a note and we can come back to it another week, once we know a little more about what's going on in those moments.
I asked him about it in the car and he wouldn't say anything either. I didn't push. I wasn't sure if I should.
Not pushing was fine. Let's pick one small thing for lunch. Theo, if we made a list of foods from easiest to hardest, crackers are the easiest, right? What's a little bit harder, but not the hardest?
Maybe the turkey sandwich. But just a bite.

Just a bite is perfect. So here's what I'm thinking. Three days this week, at school lunch, you take one bite of the turkey sandwich. You can eat crackers too. One bite. And after, you notice what happened. Did you throw up? What number were you at? Mom, can you pack half a sandwich along with the crackers?
Yes. Half a sandwich and the crackers. Should I ask him about it every day after school?
Ask once, keep it light, and write down what he tells you in the app. One bite, three days. And the bedtime plan, you answer the question once. Theo, can you say back what we're doing?
One bite of the sandwich three times. And Mom only says it once at bedtime.
He's going to hold me to that, you know.
Good, that's what we want. Great work today, Theo. You were really brave to talk about the throw-up worry. We'll see how the week goes next time.

topics: School lunch: eats only crackers or nothing; fear of throwing up in front of other kids
Bedtime: repeated 'am I going to throw up?' questions, bucket and mints by the bed, Mom stays until he is asleep
School incidents: ran to the nurse after a classmate threw up; went to a corner and covered his ears when a classmate said he felt sick
agreed: Theo takes one bite of a turkey sandwich at school lunch on three days this week; crackers still allowed
Mom packs half a sandwich along with the crackers
At bedtime Mom answers 'am I going to throw up?' once, then says 'that's the worry asking' and changes the subject
The bucket stays by the bed this week
Mom records how lunch went in the app

must_not_appear: A Fear Level for bedtime or for car rides (none was said in the session)
Removing the bucket or the mints this week
